questions.question: What is a political party?
choices: A court that reviews election disputes
An organization seeking to win elections and influence government
A government office issuing driver's licenses
A business that prints all official ballots

questions.question: What is a party platform?
choices: A statement of the party's policy positions and goals
A list of every voter in the country
A constitutional rule for counting electoral votes
A court order establishing legislative districts

questions.question: What is a party nominee?
choices: A judge appointed to oversee elections
An official who manages voter registration
A voter who refuses all party affiliation
A candidate selected to run with a party's support

questions.question: Which two parties have dominated U.S. national elections for much of modern history?
choices: Federalists and Whigs
Populists and Progressives
Democrats and Republicans
Democratic-Republicans and Know-Nothings

questions.question: What is a political coalition?
choices: Groups working together toward shared political goals
A court's final interpretation of election law
A single unchangeable set of voter opinions
A rule banning cooperation between organizations

questions.question: What does bipartisan cooperation involve?
choices: Only one party writing policy in secret
Members of two parties working together
Judges replacing elected lawmakers
Voters eliminating every party label

questions.question: What is a third party in U.S. politics?
choices: A third branch of the federal government
A court serving three states
A party outside the two dominant major parties
An agency supervising three elections

questions.question: How can parties simplify choices for voters?
choices: They guarantee that candidates hold identical views
They eliminate the need to evaluate evidence
They prevent voters from choosing independent candidates
Their labels and platforms provide information about general policy goals

questions.question: Why do parties recruit and train candidates?
choices: To develop people who can campaign and serve in office
To give candidates authority to cancel elections
To replace voter registration with party membership
To ensure every candidate serves in the judiciary

questions.question: What is a key difference between a political party and an interest group?
choices: Interest groups administer elections; parties count the votes
Parties field candidates for office; interest groups primarily seek policy influence
Parties focus on one issue; interest groups must address every issue
Interest groups write official ballots; parties enforce election laws

questions.question: How can third parties influence policy even when they do not win many offices?
choices: They can automatically appoint members of Congress
They can rewrite the Constitution without ratification
They can cancel the platforms of major parties
They can bring attention to issues adopted by other parties

questions.question: Why do broad parties often contain internal disagreements?
choices: Their voters all share the same background
Their platforms are written only by courts
They bring together people with different interests and priorities
They are prohibited from holding policy discussions

questions.question: How can single-member plurality elections encourage a two-party system?
choices: Voters and candidates may coordinate around larger parties to avoid splitting support
Every ballot legally requires exactly two names
The Constitution requires one party per legislative chamber
Small parties are automatically assigned equal seats

questions.question: What does party realignment describe?
choices: An annual change in the location of polling places
A substantial, lasting shift in party coalitions and voting patterns
A court's revision of one candidate's filing date
A temporary change in a campaign's slogan

questions.question: Why is an opposition party important in a competitive democracy?
choices: It can reject every valid election result
It can replace judicial decisions with campaign promises
It removes the need for voters to evaluate incumbents
It offers alternatives and scrutinizes the governing party

questions.question: A party platform promises a policy, but some elected members oppose it. Which conclusion is most accurate?
choices: Party platforms automatically become law
All members must have identical policy views
Platforms describe general goals without guaranteeing uniform action
The party can no longer participate in elections

questions.question: A new party emphasizes an overlooked issue, and major parties later address it. What role has the new party played?
choices: Expanding the public policy agenda
Serving as a constitutional court
Ratifying a national amendment
Administering federal tax collection

questions.question: Two parties negotiate a shared transportation bill. Which term best describes this cooperation?
choices: Judicial review
Bipartisanship
Federal supremacy
Party realignment

questions.question: Which evidence would best support a claim that a long-term party realignment occurred?
choices: One party changes the wording of a convention resolution
A candidate chooses a new campaign communications team
Several elections show a durable shift in support among major voter groups
A polling-place schedule changes for one local election

questions.question: Why should a voter examine candidates as well as their party labels?
choices: Party labels have no relationship to public policy
Candidates never differ from their party leaders
Individual qualifications are legally identical within a party
Candidates can differ in experience, priorities, and specific positions
